title: Anthropic’s Rapid But Slowing Growth Could Weigh on IPO Valuation
summary: Anthropic reported rapid-but-slowing revenue growth in a meeting with potential investors in its planned initial public offering, leaving some attendees expecting the company will need to keep its valuation target in check. At a private investor meeting Wednesday in San Francisco, the company said revenue hit $16.8 billion in the third quarter, according to people briefed on the numbers. That was a jump of about 45% from the second quarter. The figure was more than 3.6 times the company’s revenue for all of 2025. But it also represents a slower growth rate than Anthropic’s second quarter, when fevered demand for its Claude Code product drove revenue up by more than 140% from the first three months of the year.

title: Why AI-Written Software Needs a Flight Simulator
summary: As companies create more applications using AI, corporate officers say demand is rising for a new type of software that stress-tests those apps, simulating how they handle network problems and other disasters that humans may not think to test for—including cyberattacks by rogue AIs. Luis Chávez, CTO of coding assistant provider Replit, says his company uses an AI-assisted software known as a deterministic simulator, a kind of flight simulator for software. The deterministic part refers to how the simulator lets companies run the same disaster test again and again so they can try out different fixes for bugs that crop up during network failures or hacking attempts. Traditional stress-testing methods rely on developers guessing every potential problem that may arise. Merely using today’s AI models to evaluate code often produces false alarms or fake warnings, corporate executives say.

title: Nick Wingfield Promoted to Co-Executive Editor of The Information
summary: I am thrilled to announce three major editorial promotions for Nick, Abe and Meredith, along with some changes that recognize the incredible work of our newsroom and set the stage for more growth in what is shaping up to be the most exciting time in our history. Nick Wingfield has been promoted to Executive Editor , responsible for ensuring the high bar of all our reporting. Since he joined The Information eight years ago after working at the New York Times and Wall Street Journal, Nick has pushed us to think bigger in our journalism, overseeing our features efforts and some of our most important beats. When we heard whispers that Jony Ive’s personal life was becoming a distraction from his work at Apple, he and Aaron Tilley mustered a slew of reporting that turned into one of our most memorable crash leders. That’s what he has done again and again. Working with talented reporters to drive maximum impact, across coasts, beats and more. In his new role, Nick will run the day-to-day publication with me and Amir, with us all dividing up responsibilities for what we chase and ensuring the highest bar in what we publish while continuing to grow the team and build up new editorial areas. He will continue to manage his team of reporters. Abe Brown has been promoted to Features Editor, with responsibility for all our features at The Information. As Weekend editor, Abe has proven himself as something rare in media these days: a careful and skilled editor with a zest for trying new things. While managing a section, he has also jumped in any day of the week to help edit our biggest stories with a tireless work ethic and great attitude. I am excited for more reporters to work with Abe and for him to push us in new directions. I am thrilled to promote Meredith Mazilli to Finance Editor. From the day she joined The Information, it has been clear that Meredith knows finance. While she has led all sorts of consequential coverage on ads, commerce, Musk and beyond, in recent months, she has helped our finance team carve out a huge lane around the financing of data centers and this turbulent moment. I’m excited to see how far she and the team can run against that massively important story. Meredith has also begun the work of bringing new talent to the team. I am thrilled to have her officially step into the role leading Finance, continuing to expand our reporting staff and find even more lanes where we can dominate. I am also happy to share that Martin has decided he wants to shift his focus to the Briefing and future related Briefing franchises and will become Editor-at-Large . Over twelve years, Martin has had a hand in every aspect of this business. I am thrilled he will be working with us full-time to focus on writing and how to expand the Briefing franchise, while continuing to coach and advise the newsroom. And there will be more time to celebrate more than a decade of Martin as co-Executive Editor. He will continue to edit The Electric and, in the coming weeks, reporters who report to him will transition to other senior leaders to free him up to go full throttle in his new role. We are making these changes now to celebrate the success of our incredible editorial leadership team, which remains unrivaled in the industry, and to prepare for the future. The next few years are going to demand a lot of news organizations. Sweeping changes to how audiences consume news are just beginning and I honestly think most news organizations will have no idea what hit them. Meanwhile, the onslaught of “information,” much of it biased and fake, has only begun. Our secret sauce—the high impact, ahead-of-the-curve, focused work no one else is doing—is exactly the right formula for this moment.

title: CoreWeave Co-Founders’ Stock Sales Aren’t Helping Investor Confidence
summary: This was not the day to be a publicly traded neocloud (as young AI data center firms are known). As the market sold off on bad inflation data—reinforcing certainty of another interest rate hike—neoclouds tanked. These companies typically are borrowing a lot to finance expansion. The worst hit in the stock sell-off was CoreWeave, whose stock fell 15.5%, fueled by chatter that its bonds were falling to worryingly low levels. CoreWeave CEO and co-founder Michael Intrator was defiant. He told his staff, according to a spokesperson: “When you are building a new type of technology company, there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally.” Yeah, right. The issue may be more that Intrator doesn’t understand investors. He sold CoreWeave stock every week between April and the end of September, securities filings show, while his fellow co-founders have also been selling regularly. That can’t help but undermine investor confidence in the company. Intrator could win some brownie points by pledging to stop selling his stock for a while.

title: Cognition’s Plan to Limit Tokenmaxxing to the Most Efficient Engineers
summary: To rein in AI spending, large companies are capping employees’ usage, turning to cheaper and smaller models and using routers to send only the hardest requests to the most expensive models. Cognition , the startup behind the AI coding agent Devin , is adding a new trick to the book: measuring how efficiently different engineers use AI so companies can allocate more resources toward their most efficient employees, Cognition told The Information exclusively. “The limits that a user should have should not be static. They should be dynamic based on the efficiency of your usage and the value that you're getting out of it,” said Calvin Giroud , a vice president of customer engineering at Cognition. By looking at an engineer’s coding session using Devin, Cognition can estimate the equivalent number of hours it would have taken a human to do the same amount of work. Dividing by the costs of that session, Cognition gets a measure of each engineer’s efficiency.

title: Cursor Staff Investigated Whether Confidential Data Reached SpaceX for AI Training
summary: In the weeks before SpaceX’s AI unit in August introduced Grok Bot, its version of a personal AI agent, engineers at Cursor discovered a potential problem. Cursor, the AI coding startup SpaceX was then in the process of acquiring, was developing Grok Bot, and as part of that process, employees across Cursor were using the tool extensively for testing and as a part of their everyday work. In late July, engineers raised concerns that Cursor might have sent data from that internal testing—potentially including confidential information about its customers, suppliers and business partners—to SpaceX’s AI unit. One of Cursor’s lawyers warned that if word got out that the company was using the data for training, that could cause a “huge trust problem,” according to internal communications viewed by The Information.
